content.p: In July 2023, police in the Bahamas said they had stopped a plan to kill Robert Shiver, an insurance executive from Thomasville, Georgia, who played football at Auburn University. Police said they found it on a phone that had been seized in an unrelated burglary inquiry on Guana Cay, in the Abaco Islands. Police and prosecutors say the messages on that phone showed his wife, Lindsay Shiver, her alleged lover Terrance Bethel and a third man, Faron Newbold Jr., agreeing to have him killed. Robert Shiver was not hurt.

All three were charged with conspiracy to commit murder and all three have pleaded not guilty. Nobody has been convicted or acquitted. Three years after the arrests, the case is still in the pre-trial stage in the Supreme Court in Nassau, after the trial was postponed at least four times, according to WDHN.

Lindsay and Robert Shiver both attended Auburn University and lived in Thomasville, Georgia, and the family spent a good deal of time in the Bahamas, according to CNN. Robert Shiver briefly belonged to at least one NFL team, according to his company's website. The couple were in the middle of a divorce. Court filings that CNN viewed show that Robert Shiver filed on 5 April 2023 and that his wife filed the next day. He cited her "adulterous conduct"; her filing said she had "incurred debt beyond her means to pay". Fox 5 Atlanta later reported that she accused him of "physical and mental cruel treatment", including domestic violence, and that both sought primary custody of the children and sole use of the family's Georgia home.

Reports differ on the family's size and the length of the marriage. ABC News and Oxygen reported three children; a Court TV piece published by WTXL referred to two young sons in one place and three children in another. The marriage was described as 13 years old by ABC News and Fox 5 Atlanta, and as 16 years old in Oxygen's report.

On 16 July 2023, the date prosecutors give for the alleged conspiracy, Lindsay Shiver called 911 on her husband after he would not let her fly on the family's private jet to the Bahamas, according to Fox 5 Atlanta, which cited police body-camera footage it had obtained. The same outlet reported that she allegedly sent the "Kill him" message to Newbold that day.

The investigation began with a break-in at Grabber's Bar and Grill on Guana Cay. Police searched the phone of a suspect in that case, according to Oxygen, which cited Bahamas Court News, and came across WhatsApp messages about a plan to kill Robert Shiver. CNN reported that the identity of the phone's owner remained unclear. WDHN reported that the messages allegedly included photographs of Robert Shiver and the words "Kill him".

ABC News reported, from a court document it obtained, that Bahamian authorities say Lindsay Shiver admitted in a police interview to sending the message "Kill him" and photographs of her husband to the man alleged to be the hired killer, Newbold. The same report said Bethel became a suspect in the burglary and that detectives then told Robert Shiver of the plot. According to the Thomasville Times-Enterprise, which cited the prosecutor's initial report, he asked the police to act because he feared for his own life and the lives of the children. The police report, as quoted by Oxygen from the Times-Enterprise, said the three, together at Abaco on 16 July 2023, "with a common purpose" agreed to commit the murder of Robert Shiver.

The three were arrested and flown to Nassau. At their first appearance, on a Friday in late July 2023, they were not asked to plead and were remanded to a corrections facility until a hearing on 5 October, according to CNN. Court documents in the Bahamas misidentified Robert Shiver as "Richard Shiver", CNN noted. A few days later a Supreme Court judge set bail at $100,000 in cash for Lindsay Shiver, with an ankle monitor, and $20,000 each for Bethel and Newbold, with a curfew, WTVY reported, citing the Bahamian outlet Our News.
content.h2: Pleas and a string of lost trial dates
content.p: On 8 December 2023 the three stood in a Bahamian courtroom, arms folded, and each told the judge they were not guilty, according to Court TV's reporter, who was present. They were represented by one lawyer, Owen Wells, and were to be tried together. Wells said: "Lindsay is innocent and the evidence will clearly demonstrate her innocence." Court TV reported that the three had presented a united front, saying they had never seriously planned to kill Lindsay Shiver's husband. Robert Shiver, appearing by video link in a hearing that month, told the judge he was "thankful to be alive", Fox 5 Atlanta reported.

The judge set trial for 4 March 2024, then reset it for 1 July 2024. Three days before the July date, NewsNation reported that the trial would not go ahead and that no new date had been fixed. Another date, 29 August 2025, was lost too; WDHN counted it as the fourth postponement, said no reason had been given and reported a new date of 2 March 2026. No trial has been reported to have begun on that date or since. If convicted, each defendant could face between 30 and 60 years in prison, according to NewsNation.
content.h2: Bail, a television interview and a gag order
content.p: Lindsay Shiver's bail was varied in December 2023 so that she could travel to the United States, on condition that she lived at an address in Abbeville, Alabama, and entered Georgia only for custody and divorce proceedings, according to The Tribune. Her original conditions included an 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew, a distance of at least 100 feet from Robert Shiver and witnesses, and a ban on foreign travel without the court's permission.

In early October 2024 Bethel gave an interview to Good Morning America, which also featured footage of Shiver. "Nobody ever wanted him dead," Bethel said in it, according to WDHN. "I'm definitely not guilty of conspiracy to commit murder, and Faron's not guilty of being a hired hitman." In late October, Senior Justice Cheryl Grant-Thompson revoked bail for both Shiver and Bethel, and they were taken into custody in Nassau, according to The Tribune and WDHN. The judge called the interview a "blatant disregard for the court's leniency and indulgence" and "a spit in the face of justice". Prosecutors had filed affidavits, including one from Robert Shiver listing trips to Florida, alleging that she had left Alabama without the court's permission, and the judge rejected the defence argument that no condition had been breached. According to The Tribune, she also said she was taking Shiver "out of harm's way" after a report that another boyfriend had tried to suffocate her at her home in Alabama. According to The Tribune, prosecutors said Bethel had missed sign-in requirements 12 times and had also given interviews to foreign television stations.

Fox 5 Atlanta reported in February 2025 that the judge had reversed the decision, on condition that Shiver and Bethel kept silent under a gag order, and that Shiver was expected to be released on $100,000 bail.

The most recent hearings, in 2026, concerned the monitoring device rather than the alleged plot. Shiver had applied to have it removed because it was causing blisters on her ankle; the judge ordered it refitted rather than taken off, according to The Nassau Guardian. Prosecutor Karine MacVean said Shiver first reported a fault on 22 December 2025 and that her movements went unmonitored for 126 days, until the device was replaced in May. The defence lawyer, Terrel Butler, said Shiver had phoned in twice a day under an agreed alternative, had been ill with norovirus when a servicing appointment was proposed, and had five ankle monitors that all developed problems. Migrafill's witness agreed that an alternative arrangement existed and that the company required Shiver to travel to Florida, and The Tribune noted that a Migrafill representative had previously testified that several of the devices Shiver wore had malfunctioned.

On 27 August 2026 Justice Grant-Thompson dismissed the prosecution's application to revoke bail. She found that Shiver had called in as requested, was not a flight risk and had complied with her conditions, but told her that phone calls alone were not enough and that electronic monitoring would stay. In her view the monitor was a tracking tool for an accused person, not an accessory, and she hoped a slimmer replacement would end its "tortured history of malfunctioning".

As of late August 2026, the three remain charged and presumed innocent, with no verdict. What the public knows of the messages comes from what police and prosecutors have said they contain, and the defence disputes that any real plan existed.
